body.text: Udīcya Śyāmilaka: Pāḍatāḍitaka
body.translated_text: <s>Udīcya Śyāmilaka</s>: <s>Pādatāḍitaka</s> (The Kick)

body.text:
[p.65] 0 śrīmahākaviśyāmilakaviracitaṃ pādatāḍitakam.
(nāndyante, tataḥ praviśati sūtradhāraḥ)
(sūtra#)
l (a) dehatyāgena śambhor nayanahutavahe mānito yena kopaḥ
(b) sendrā yasyānuśiṣṭiṃ srajam iva vibudhā dhārayanty uttamāṅgaiḥ
(c) pāyāt kāmaḥ sa yuṣmān pravitatavanitālocanāpāṅgaśārṅgo
(d) bāṇā yasyendriyārthā munijanamanasāṃ sādakā bhedakāś ca
api ca
2 (a) sabhrūkṣepaṃ sahāsaṃ stananihitakarām īkṣamāṇena devīṃ
(b) saṃtrāsākṣiptavāgbhiḥ saha gaṇapatibhir nandinā vanditena
(c) pāyād vaḥ puṣpaketur vṛṣapatikakudāpāśrayanyastadoṣṇā
(d) yasya kruddhena bāhyaṃ karaṇam apahṛtaṃ śambhunā na prabhāvaḥ
evam āryamiśrān śirasā praṇipatya vijñāpayāmi yad vayam āryaśyāmilakasya kṛtiṃ pādatāḍitakaṃ nāma bhāṇaṃ prayoktuṃ
body.translated_text: The <s>Pādatāḍitaka</s>, composed by the illustrious great poet <s>Śyāmilaka</s>. (After the benedictory verse (<s>nāndī</s>), the stage-manager (<s>sūtradhāra</s>) enters.) (Stage-manager:) [Verse 1:] May <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love), whose anger was honored by <s>Śambhu</s> (Śiva) through the sacrifice of [Kāma's] body in the fire of [Śiva's] eye, whose command the gods including <s>Indra</s> bear upon their heads like a garland, who has the sidelong glances of women's eyes spread wide as his bow (<s>śārṅga</s>), and whose arrows — the objects of the senses — are both accomplishers and destroyers of the minds of sages — may he protect you! And furthermore: [Verse 2:] May <s>Puṣpaketu</s> (the flower-bannered one, i.e., <s>Kāma</s>), who was gazed upon by [<s>Pārvatī</s>] the goddess with a frown and a smile, her hand placed on her breast, while <s>Nandin</s> bowed and the <s>Gaṇapati</s>s (attendant lords) uttered words startled with alarm, whose arm was resting on the hump of the bull-lord (<s>Vṛṣapati</s>, i.e., <s>Śiva</s>'s bull), and whose external faculties alone — not his power — were taken away by the angered <s>Śambhu</s> — may he protect you! Having thus bowed my head before the honorable assembly, I inform [you] that we are about to perform the <s>bhāṇa</s> (monologue play) called <s>Pādatāḍitaka</s>, a composition of the noble <s>Śyāmilaka</s>,

body.text:
[p.66] vyavasitāḥ tat tasya kaver matipariśramam avadhānadānenānugrahītum icchāmaḥ kutaḥ
3 (a) idam iha padaṃ mā bhūd evaṃ bhavatv idam anyathā
(b) kṛtam idam ayaṃ granthenārtho mahān upapāditaḥ
(c) iti manasi yaḥ kāvyārambhe kaver bhavati śramaḥ
(d) sanayanajalo romodbhedaḥ satāṃ tam apohati
kutaḥ
4 (a) nirgamyatāṃ bakabiḍālasamapracārair
(b) āryaiś ca rājasacivaiḥ śamavṛttibhiś ca
(c) tiṣṭhantu ḍiṇḍikavinarmakalāvidagdhā
(d) nirmakṣikaṃ madhu pipāsati dhūrtagoṣṭhī
kutaḥ
5 (a) na prāpnuvanti yatayo ruditena mokṣaṃ
(b) svargāyatiṃ na parihāsakathā ruṇaddhi
(c) tasmāt pratītamanasā hasitavyam eva
(d) vṛttiṃ budhena khalu kaurukucīṃ vihāya
ko nu khalu mayi vijñāpanāvyagre śabda iva śrūyate (karṇaṃ dattvā) hanta vijñātam eṣa hi sa viṭamaṇḍapaṃ praviśya dhūrtacākrikaḥ khalatiśyāmilako ghaṇṭām āhatya ghoṣayati ya eṣaḥ
body.translated_text: and we are resolved [to do so]. We desire to honor the intellectual labor of that poet by the gift of [your] attention. Why? [Verse 3:] 'Let not this word be thus; let this be otherwise; this has been done; by this construction a great meaning has been established' — the toil that [arises] in the poet's mind at the commencement of a literary work, the goosebumps [of appreciation] accompanied by tears of the good-hearted dispel it. Why? [Verse 4:] Let the noble ones, the king's ministers who conduct themselves with the deceit of herons and cats yet [assume] the demeanor of tranquility, depart! Let those skilled in the art of jesting with buffoons remain — the assembly of rogues thirsts for honey free from flies. Why? [Verse 5:] Ascetics do not attain liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) by weeping, nor does comic storytelling obstruct [one's] future heavenly [destiny]. Therefore, with a trusting mind, one should indeed laugh, abandoning, as a wise person [should], the hypocritical way of life. Now, while I am busy with my announcement, a sound as it were is heard. (Listening.) Ah, I understand! For here, having entered the rogues' pavilion (<s>viṭamaṇḍapa</s>), that trickster, the bald-headed <s>Śyāmilaka</s>, is striking the bell and proclaiming — this one here —

body.text:
[p.67] 6 (a) vyatikarasukhabhedaḥ kāminīkāmukānāṃ
(b) divasasamayadūto dundubhīnāṃ purodhāḥ
(c) kalam uṣasi kharatvād yasya kaṇṭhīravāṇāṃ
(d) balavad abhinadanto gardabhā nānuyānti
kiṃ ca tāvad anena ghuṣyate (karṇaṃ dattvā) (naipathye)
7 (a) jayati madanasya ketuḥ
 kāntaṃ praty udyato vilāsinyāḥ
 (b) śirasā prārthayitavyaḥ
 sālaktakanūpuraḥ pādaḥ
 (niṣkrāntaḥ)
 (sthāpanā)
 (tataḥ praviśati viṭaḥ)
 vi -- mā tāvad bhoḥ -- kim atra ghoṣayitavyam yad evam
 8 (a) praṇayakalahodyatena
 srastāṃśukadarśitorumūlena
 (b) jitam eva madakalāyā
 nūpuramukhareṇa pādena
aye kenaitad dhasitam (vilokya) dadruṇamādhavo 'py atraiva aṃgho dadruṇamādhava kim atra hāsyasthānam kiṃ bravīṣi - pratyakṣaṃ hi me tad yad atīte 'hani tatrabhavatyā surāṣṭrāṇāṃ vāramukhyayā samadanayā madanasenikayā tatrabhavāṃs tauṇḍikokir viṣṇunāgaś caraṇakamalena śirasy anugṛhīta iti suṣṭhu khalv idam ucyate - eti jīvantam ānando naraṃ varṣaśatād
body.translated_text: [Verse 6:] He who is the divider of the mutual pleasures of lovers and beloved women, the herald of daytime, the priest of kettledrums, at dawn, due to [their] harshness, the donkeys, braying loudly, do not follow after the soft [sounds] of his throat-born lions. And what is he now announcing? (Listening.) (From offstage:) [Verse 7:] Victorious is the foot of the coquette, raised toward her lover — the banner of <s>Madana</s> (the god of love), to be entreated with bowed head, adorned with lac-dyed anklets! (Exit.) (Transitional interlude.) (Then the libertine (<s>viṭa</s>) enters.) Libertine: Stop, sirs! What is there to announce here? For thus — [Verse 8:] Victory indeed belongs to the foot, clamorous with anklets, of the woman intoxicated with passion, [her foot] raised in a quarrel of love, [her] garment slipping to reveal the root of [her] thigh. Ah, who laughed at this? (Looking around.) <s>Dadruṇamādhava</s> is also right here. Hey, <s>Dadruṇamādhava</s>, what is there to laugh about? What do you say? — For I personally [witnessed] what [happened] yesterday: the honorable chief courtesan of the <s>Surāṣṭra</s>s, <s>Samadanā Madanasenikā</s>, graced the honorable <s>Tauṇḍikoki Viṣṇunāga</s> upon the head with [her] lotus-foot! Well indeed is this said: 'Joy comes to a man who lives, even after a hundred years.'

body.text:
[p.68] apīti viṣṇunāgo 'pi nāmaivaṃ sarvakāmijanasādhāraṇaṃ caraṇatāḍanasaṃjñakaṃ śirasy abhiṣekaṃ prāptavān kiṃ bravīṣikuto 'sya tāni bhāgadheyāni yaḥ sa īdṛśānāṃ praṇayakalahotsavānāṃ pātraṃ bhaviṣyati sa hi tasyā veśadevatāyās taṃ saṃmānaviśeṣam avamānaṃ manyamānaḥ krodhaparivyaktanayanarāgaḥ prasphuritabhrukuṭīvakraṃ lalāṭaṃ kṛtvā śiro vinirdhūya daśanair oṣṭham abhidaśya pāṇinā pāṇim abhihatya dīrghaṃ niḥśvasyoktavān hā dhik puṃścali, anātmajñe, yayā tvayā mamāsmin
9 (a) prayatakarayā mātrā yatnāt prabaddhaśikhaṇḍake
(b) caraṇavinate pitrāghrāte śiśur guṇavān iti
(c) sakusumalavaiḥ śāntyambhobhir dvijātibhir ukṣite
(d) śirasi caraṇo nyasto garvān na gauravam īkṣitam
evaṃ cānenoktā virajyamānasaṃdhyārāgeva rajani varṇāntaram upagatā atiprabhātacandraniṣprabhaṃ vadanam udvahantī 10 (a) vyapagatamadarāgā bhraśyamānopacārā
(b) kim idam iti viṣādāt svinnasarvāṅgayaṣṭiḥ
(c) bhayavigalitaśobhā vāntapuṣpeṇa mūrdhnā
(d) na punar iti vadantī pādayos tasya lagnā
praṇipātāvanatā cānena nirdhūyoktā carṣaṇi, mā sprākṣīḥ, kardanena na māṃ ḍhaukitum arhasīti kaṣṭaṃ bhoḥ, kokilā khalu kauśikam anuvartate madanasenikāpi taṃ puruṣavetālaṃ
body.translated_text:
[p.68] Indeed! So even <s>Viṣṇunāga</s> received that consecration — called a 'foot-kick to the head' — which is common to all lovers! What do you say? From where could he have such good fortune, that he should become the object of such festivals of lovers' quarrels? For he, considering that special honor from the courtesan-goddess to be an insult, with eyes reddened by anger, making his forehead crooked with furrowed brows, shaking his head, biting his lip with his teeth, slapping one hand against the other, and sighing deeply, said: 'Shame on you, wanton woman! Self-ignorant creature! You who upon me —
(9a) Upon this head, on which my mother with careful hands painstakingly tied the top-knot,
(9b) which was bowed at the feet and smelled by my father, [who said] "the child is virtuous,"
(9c) which was sprinkled with flower-scented waters of benediction by <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> —
(9d) upon this head a foot was placed out of arrogance, without regard for its dignity!'
And she, thus addressed by him, like an evening twilight whose color fades, having assumed a different complexion, bearing a face as lusterless as the moon at deep dawn:
(10a) With the flush of passion gone, her attentions failing,
(10b) [thinking] 'What is this?' — her entire body perspiring from distress,
(10c) her beauty dissolved by fear, her head [now empty] as if its flowers had been vomited forth,
(10d) saying 'Never again!' — she clung to his feet.
And though she fell prostrate, he shook her off and said: 'Wretch! Don't touch me! You don't deserve to approach me with your filth!' Alas! A cuckoo indeed follows an owl — and <s>Madanasenikā</s> too follows that living corpse of a man,

body.text:
[p.69] kadaryam apavīryam anuvartata iti bhavati me vismayaḥ bhavati ca punar mahāmātraputro rājñaḥ śāsanādhikṛta iti dānakāmāv upekṣate śabdakāmāḥ khalv etā bhavanti kāme hi prayojanam anekavidham ity upadiśyate kiṃ bravīṣi - labdhaṃ khalu śabdakāmayā śabdapradhānārjanāc chabdasya vyasanam iti sā hi tapasvinī
11 (a) tiryaktrapāvanatapakṣmapuṭapravāntair
(b) dhautādharastanamukhī nayanāmbupātaiḥ
(c) svāṅgeṣv alīyata navaiḥ sahasā stanadbhir
(d) udvejitā jaladharair iva rājahaṃsī iti
na ca bhoḥ citram idaṃ śrotavyaṃ śrutam na ca khalv asmābhir viditārthair apy atītaṃ pṛṣṭam tatas tataḥ kiṃ bravīṣi-- tataḥ sa mayā nirbhartsyoktaḥ: aye vaiyākaraṇakhasūcin, sumanaso musalena mā kṣautsīr vallakīm ulmukena mā vādīr, vākkṣureṇa kisalayaklībāṃ mā cchetsīr mattakāśinīm iti evam ukto mām anādṛtya viṭamahattarabhaṭṭijīmūtagṛhaṃ gataḥ tataḥ sā
body.translated_text:
[p.69] that miser, that impotent fellow! My amazement is great. And moreover, being the son of a chief minister and appointed to royal authority, he disdains those who desire to give — for these [courtesans] are fame-seekers indeed. It is taught that there are many kinds of purposes in desire. What do you say? — Well, the fame-seeking woman has indeed obtained this: from pursuing fame as the chief goal, she has gained the ruin of [her] reputation! For that poor woman:
(11a) With sidelong, shame-lowered eyelashes' edges streaming,
(11b) her lower breast and face washed by the cascading tears from her eyes,
(11c) she cowered within her own limbs, suddenly startled
(11d) by fresh thunderclouds — like a royal goose.
And sir, this is no wonder to be heard — it has been heard before! Nor was it asked by us who already know the matter. Then what? What do you say? — Then he was rebuked by me: 'Listen, you grammarian-needle-picker! Don't pound flowers with a pestle! Don't play a lute with a firebrand! Don't cut the tender-sprout that is the delicate woman with the razor of your tongue!' Though thus addressed, disregarding me, he went to the house of the great courtesan-patron <s>Bhaṭṭi Jīmūta</s>. Then she,

body.text:
[p.70] tapasvinī karakisalayaparyastakapolam ānanaṃ kṛtvā praruditā tata utthāpya mayoktā: sundari, na vānaro veṣṭanam arhati, gardabho vā varapravahaṇaṃ voḍhum alam alaṃ ruditena hāsyaḥ khalv eṣa tapasvī naivaṃ mahāntaṃ śiraḥsatkāram arhati
12 (a) kiṃ kāmī na kacagrahair yam abalāḥ kliśyanti mattā balād
(b) yaṃ badhnanti na mekhalābhir athavā na ghnanti karṇotpalaiḥ
(c) pakṣe tasya tu manmathaḥ sukṛtinas tasyotsavo yauvanaṃ
(d) dāseneva rahasy apetavinayāḥ krīḍanti yenāṅganāḥ
evaṃ coktā smitapuraḥsaram apāṅgena me vacaḥ pratigṛhya saśiraḥpādam avakuṇṭhya vāsasā śayanatalam alaṃkṛtavatī aham api kāmipratyavarasya duścaritam anucintayan prabhātam - iti rajñaḥ prabhātanāndīsvanair utthāpitaḥ kṛtakartavyas tad eva duḥsvapnadarśanam ivāpanetuṃ brāhmaṇapīṭhikāṃ gataḥ tasyāṃ ca brāhmaṇapīṭhikāyāṃ pūrvagataṃ kīrṇakeśaṃ viṣṇunā-
body.translated_text:
[p.70] the poor woman, placing her cheek upon the bud of her hand, began to weep. Then, raising her up, I said: 'Fair one, a monkey does not deserve a wreath, nor is a donkey fit to draw a fine carriage. Enough of weeping! That pathetic fellow is truly laughable — he does not deserve such great honor to his head.
(12a) What lover is there whom amorous women do not torment by seizing his hair,
(12b) whom they do not bind with their girdle-strings, or do not strike with lotus-blossoms behind the ear?
(12c) On whose side is the god of love? That fortunate one — for him youth is a festival!
(12d) Women, their modesty abandoned in private, sport with him as with a slave.'
And she, thus addressed, receiving my words with a sidelong glance preceded by a smile, covering herself from head to foot with her garment, adorned her bed. I too, having pushed away the lover's misconduct and reflecting upon it, [waited for] dawn. — Then, awakened by the sounds of the king's morning benediction, having performed my morning duties, I went to the Brāhmaṇa-assembly-hall as if to dispel a bad dream. And in that assembly-hall, [I found] <s>Viṣṇunāga</s>, who had arrived earlier, with disheveled hair —

body.text:
[p.71] gam evārtarūpam ātmakarmācakṣamāṇam asāv ahaṃ bhoḥ evaṃkarmā taṃ mā vṛṣalyāḥ pādāvadhūtaśiraskaṃ trātum arhanti traividyavṛddhā ity uktavantam apaśyam evaṃ coktā brāhmaṇāś calakapolasūcitahāsam anyonyam avalokya muhūrtam iva dhyātvoktavantaḥ bhoḥ sādho, avalokitāny asmābhir manuyamavasiṣṭhagautamabharadvājaśaṅkhalikhitāpastambahārītapraceto devalavṛddhagārgyaprabhṛtīnāṃ maharṣīṇāṃ dharmaśāstrāṇi nāsyaivaṃvidhasya mahataḥ pātakasya prāyaścittam avagacchāma iti evaṃ cokto viṣaṇṇataravaktra ucchritya hastāv upākrośat bho bhoḥ, caturtho varṇa iti na mām arhatha bhūmidevāḥ parityaktum kutaḥ
13 (a) āryo 'smi śuddhacarito 'smi kulodgato 'smi
(b) śabde ca hetusamaye ca kṛtaśramo 'smi
(c) rājño 'smi śāsanakaro na pṛthagjano 'smi
(d) trāyadhvam ārtam agatiṃ śaraṇāgato 'smi
 evaṃ coktāyāṃ tasyāṃ pariṣadi
body.translated_text: [p.71] I saw him in a pitiable state, confessing his own deed, saying: 'I, sirs, am one who has done such a deed; may the elders learned in the three <s>Vedas</s> deign to save me, whose head has been kicked by the foot of a <s>vṛṣalī</s> (low-caste woman).' And when thus addressed, the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, glancing at one another with smiles betrayed by trembling cheeks, pondered for a moment and said: 'Good sir, we have examined the <s>dharmaśāstras</s> (law-texts) of the great sages — <s>Manu</s>, <s>Yama</s>, <s>Vasiṣṭha</s>, <s>Gautama</s>, <s>Bharadvāja</s>, <s>Śaṅkhalikhita</s>, <s>Āpastamba</s>, <s>Hārīta</s>, <s>Pracetas</s>, <s>Devala</s>, <s>Vṛddhagārgya</s>, and others — yet we cannot find a <s>prāyaścitta</s> (penance) for such a great sin as this.' When thus told, with an even more dejected face, he raised his hands and cried out: 'Sirs, sirs! Just because I am of the fourth <s>varṇa</s> (class), you gods of the earth should not abandon me! For — (verse 13) I am noble, I am of pure conduct, I am born of good family, I have labored in grammar and logic, I execute the king's commands, I am no common man — save this afflicted one who has no refuge; I have come seeking shelter!' When he had spoken thus in that assembly,

body.text:
[p.72] 14 (a) kaiścid gaur ayam ity aratnicalanair anyonyam āghaṭṭitaṃ
(b) syād unmatta iti sthitaṃ smitamukhaiḥ kaiścic ciraṃ vīkṣitam
(c) kaiścit kāmapiśāca ity api tṛṇaṃ dattvāntare dhikkṛtaḥ
(d) kaiścid duṣkṛtakāriṇīti ca punaḥ saivāṅganā śocitā
evamavasthāyāṃ ca saṃsadi tasyāṃ pratipattimūḍheṣu brāhmaṇeṣu prāyaścittavipralambhavihvale krośati viṣṇunāge teṣām ekatama ācāryaputraḥ svayaṃ cācāryo daṇḍanītyānvīkṣikyor anyāsu ca vidyāsv abhivinītaḥ kalāsv api ca sarvāsu paraṃ kauśalam anuprāpto vāgmī cāntevāsigaṇaparivṛtaḥ parihāsaprakṛtiḥ śāṇḍilyo bhavasvāmī nāma brāhmaṇaḥ savyetaraṃ hastam udyamya smitodagrayā vācā pariṣadam āmantryoktavān aye bho viṣṇunāga, na bhetavyam alam alaṃ viṣādena astīdaṃ dharmavacanaṃ yathā deśajātikulatīrthasamayadharmāś cāmnāyair aviruddhāḥ pramāṇam iti ato viṭajātiṃ saṃnipātya viṭamukhyebhyaḥ prāyaścittaṃ mṛgyatām te hi tvām asmāt kilbiṣān mocayiṣyanti ity ukte sādhuvādānuyātram ūrdhvāṅgulipranṛttam avartata
body.translated_text: [p.72] (verse 14) By some he was nudged with elbow-jabs, muttering to each other 'This one is an ox!'; by some he was stared at for a long time, their faces smiling, thinking 'He must be mad'; by some he was ridiculed with a blade of grass placed before him, calling him a 'lust-demon'; and by some that same woman was pitied, saying 'She who did wrong.' In that assembly, at this impasse, while the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> were perplexed about what to do, and while <s>Viṣṇunāga</s> was crying out, distraught at the failure to find a penance — one among them, a son of a teacher and himself a teacher, well-versed in jurisprudence and logic and trained in other sciences as well, having attained the highest skill in all arts, eloquent, surrounded by a host of disciples, and humorous by nature — a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> of the <s>Śāṇḍilya</s> lineage named <s>Bhavasvāmin</s>, raising his right hand and addressing the assembly in a voice brimming with a smile, said: 'Ho, <s>Viṣṇunāga</s>, do not fear! Enough, enough of despair! There is this precept of <s>dharma</s>: that the customs of region, caste, family, pilgrimage place, and convention, when not contradicted by the sacred traditions, are authoritative. Therefore, convene the <s>viṭa</s> community and seek a penance from the <s>viṭa</s> elders, for they will free you from this sin.' When this was said, a dance of raised fingers arose, accompanied by cries of 'Well said!'

body.text:
[p.73] tasyāṃ pariṣadi tac chrutvā viṣṇunāgo 'py anugṛhīta iti prasthitaḥ tvaṃ cāpi viṭasaṃnipātakarmaṇi niyukta iti bāḍham. kiṃ bravīṣi - ke punar iha bhavato viṭāḥ saṃmatā iti nanu bhavān eva tāvad agre viṭaḥ kiṃ bravīṣi - katham aham api nāma viṭaśabdenānugṛhīta iti kaḥ saṃśayaḥ? śrūyatām
15 (a) divasam akhilaṃ kṛtvā vādaṃ saha vyavahāribhir
(b) divasavigame bhuktvā bhojyaṃ suhṛdbhavane kvacit

body.translated_text: [p.86] (verses 36-39) This one placates her angry lover; that one, placated by her lover, relents. That one, striking the seven strings with her nails, yearning, cries out sweetly in a melody resembling the fifth note of the <s>kākalī</s> scale, under the pretext of beautiful song. This one, mirror placed before her, is being adorned by her lover; that beloved woman ties her lover's hair-knot. That one teaches a <s>śārikā</s> (mynah bird) to speak clearly; this one, intoxicated — a peacock threatened by her with a mango blossom — dances. How this one wearies her waist with excessive ball-play! That one, little one, seated with her lover, plays at dice; and this mature one — by her a painting is being drawn by her own hand; that one recites a tale in turn. 'Enough, enough of such haste — sit down, dear lady! It has been long since you were seen!' What do you say? — 'You should ask him today, by whom I, the naive one, was so deceived.' 'You shall be appeased! Blessings upon you! We shall accomplish everything by all means.'

[p.87] (Walking about.) Here another haven of friends has appeared! For here is that <s>Bālhika Kāṅkāyana</s>, the physician <s>Aiśānacandri Hariścandra</s> — like the moon illuminating the lotus-pond of the courtesan-quarter — approaching from this direction. What could his purpose here be? (Reflecting.) Ah, I know! He desires <s>Priyaṅguyaṣṭikā</s>, the sister of <s>Yaśomatī</s>, his former lover. He also secretly deceives us. So it's impossible to pass him by without confronting him — let me approach. (Approaching.) O you solitary <s>cakravāka</s> bird of the lotus-thicket of the courtesan-quarter, where are you coming from? What do you say? — 'I am coming from having treated your dear friend's younger sister <s>Priyaṅguyaṣṭikā</s> with medicine.' Surely the fire of passion in her — for whom love-making is abundant — has not fallen ill; have you prescribed a digestive for it? What do you say? — 'Set aside the jokes. Her headache is serious indeed.' Friend, what is true [about that]? What do you say? — 'What doubt is there? It is difficult to cure.' Just so! For 'headache' is the courtesan-folk's go-to pretended illness. See for yourself:
(40a) Placing on her forehead sandalwood paste resembling blood,

(41b) who holds up with her hand at the navel her garment slipping with its girdle,

What do you say? — 'Friend, just so, it shall be done.' You rogue! [But only] if you don't secretly mock us again! What do you say? — Then, my friend: [Verse 48:] As I stood before her, her hips, by the loosening of her girdle, [became] a more distinctly visible orb; with [her] two hands, being bashful, she closed my eyes! Shame on you, you braggart! You have become a source of disgust and an object of censure among respectable people! What do you say? — 'Even so, I am honored! Have you not heard [this] in the <s>Mahābhārata</s>? [Verse 49:] He whose enemies are not many, from whom people are not disturbed, whom they do not censure upon meeting — he, O <s>Pārtha</s>, is the lowest of men.' Well, sir, this is indeed the nature of a buffoon (<s>ḍiṇḍi</s>)! Even so — well done, sir! I am delighted by this buffoonery of yours. In every way, you deserve sovereignty among the libertines. Now here is the benediction. What do you say? — 'I am attentive.' Then listen: [Verse 50:] At dawn, understanding [that it is morning], having embraced the back of you while you sleep, having boldly mounted your side, with one thigh uncovered by her garment, then seizing your hair and turning your lotus-face toward her, may your beloved drink and make you drink the nectar of her own lips!

body.translated_text: [p.93] This one, saying 'I am honored!' — runs off. Salutations to the lord; let us proceed then. (Walking about.) Ah, who indeed is this [woman] adorning the view of her own mansion like an <s>Apsaras</s> (celestial nymph) adorning a heavenly chariot? This is indeed the chief courtesan of the <s>Kāśī</s>s, the warrior-woman named <s>Sukhamati</s>, who, playing a <s>piñcholā</s> (flute), graces the eye with the charms of her beauty, grace, and coquetry. How wonderful! (verse 51) With her breast-burden bound by a golden sash, her broad hips frankly displayed by a garment reaching mid-thigh, she moves about, agitating the minds of lovers — this one, swaying like a tendril of the pleasure-quarter's vine. Moreover — (verse 52) Her face anointed with the shadow of a single earring-jewel slipping past her cheek, with sighs — betrayed by the sound 'hī' — greedy for a downward breath, repeatedly exhaled, as she places the sweet <s>piñcholā</s> to her lip and plays it — the household peacock, mistaking it for the croaking of a frog, circles around her with his face turned askance. Now what is this? From the residence of <s>Indrasvāmin</s>, that fellow's confidential servant <s>Hiraṇyagarbhaka</s> has just now emerged and is coming this way. What wonder is there in this? <s>Indrasvāmin</s>, <s>Hiraṇyagarbhaka</s>, and the pleasure-quarter — this is a fitting combination, like 'what is hot joined with what is hot!' Here he approaches me with folded hands. Hey, <s>Hiraṇyagarbhaka</s>! Is this temple of the pleasure-quarter deity to be demolished by border-barbarians?

body.translated_text: [p.94] What do you say? — 'I am indeed my master's [servant]; I have been yoked to this task by his passion for a foreign [woman]. For she formerly charges five hundred gold pieces; now, even when invited with a thousand, even when her own mother is employed [as persuader], she cannot be brought to the bathing-ford [i.e., to yield]. Therefore, you too should deign to bring her around.' You are altogether too straightforward! For not even with a hundred thousand [gold pieces] can lives be bought. What do you say? — 'And what reason for danger to her life do you see in our case?' Indeed, it has been revealed that the honorable lady's fan-bearer, the servant <s>Kuṭaṅgadāsī</s>, experienced such a scandal from her master's association! What do you say? — 'Touch this body of mine — it is the truth.' An honest man should not speak thus to his master with falsehood. What do you say? — 'This is indeed the long-standing practice of our master.' That is precisely why it cannot be made otherwise. But that is not so — look, sir: (verse 53) Skilled in <s>kāvya</s> (poetry), <s>gāndharva</s> (music), and the science of dance, competent, generous, courteous, a <s>Dākṣiṇātya</s> (southerner) — what courtesan would not desire as her patron the lord of the <s>Koṅkaṇas</s>, were it not for his compulsive affliction with women due to his candor? And moreover, she, claiming the <s>Pāraśava Kauśika Siṃhavarman</s>, the brother-in-law of our king, as her friend, puts all lovers to shame with her refusals. What do you say? — 'And why does she thus disdain him out of excessive passion?' What is appropriate to your region indeed is perpetual over-indulgence! What do you say? — 'I do not understand what is appropriate or inappropriate to the region — let it be stated plainly.' Very well, since I am thus honored, how shall I not tell? In every way, there is no glory without a demon [behind it]! Or rather, he alone is justified in touring foreign lands. Why? (verse 60a) For having placed his feet upon the heads of the kings of the <s>Aparānta</s>s, <s>Śaka</s>s, <s>Mālava</s>s, and [other] rulers, (60b) roaming as he pleased, (60c) having come in due time to [his] mother and mother <s>Gaṅgā</s>, (60d) he has revealed the glory of the <s>Magadha</s> royal family. (verse 62, in <s>Prākṛt</s>:) (62a) 'He is not human!' says the noble one; (62b) 'by his birth-lineage, no one desires [to rival] him; (62c) not even gold, O friend, [matches] his accomplishments of action' — (62d) for the <s>viṭa</s>s indeed savor the accomplishment of fine taste.

body.translated_text: [p.98] (Walking about.) Here he is inscribing the victory-banner of the temple of <s>Pradyumnadeva</s> (the god of love). That is <s>ḍiṇḍi</s>-behavior! For these <s>ḍiṇḍi</s>s are not very far removed from monkeys! And what is his fondness for <s>ḍiṇḍi</s>s anyway? For <s>ḍiṇḍi</s>s — (verse 63a) they destroy paintings with their own smearings, (63b) they deposit brush-and-ink filth on palace walls, (63c) taking a sharp-edged iron implement, (63d) they go about on palace floors making worm-like engravings. And what is he now writing? (Looking.) '<s>Nirapekṣa</s>' ('Indifferent'). His name is apt indeed! How rightly it is said — 'a name brings misfortune to one's character.' For this villain, through his indifference, emaciated our dear friend as if by the vow of a pleasure-quarter ascetic. For that poor woman — (verse 64a) With tears from her eyes [streaming] through eyelash-tips curving dark and thick, (64b) with a face [dabbed by] a hand whose bangles are washed by those eye-tears, (64c) she bears heavy sorrow equally with her heart — (64d) she of the three folds, threefold in three ways, her hair-line made crooked [by grief]. I shall reproach him then. Ho, lord <s>Nirapekṣa</s>! For you who walks professing compassion and friendship — is it proper to be so neglectful toward the woman who is devoted to you? What do you say? — 'The meaning of the deception has been understood; I have been touched by becoming a devotee — such is the way of the world (<s>saṃsāra</s>).'

body.translated_text: 'Thus spoke the <s>Tathāgata</s> (the Buddha).' Come now, sir — is the word of the blessed <s>Tathāgata</s> authoritative only in that [matter] and not elsewhere? What do you say? — 'Where or when has the word of the <s>Tathāgata</s> been without authority for me?' Is that your assertion? What do you say? — 'What doubt is there?' Fair-faced one, listen: [Verse 65:] Having observed a deer that has come thus — its tongue lolling from exhaustion, its face upturned, an arrow lodged firmly in its heart — do you not remember a deer that came thus (<s>tathāgata</s>)? He has laughed. What do you say? — 'Indeed, the teaching of the <s>Tathāgata</s> should not be doubted; for one thing is the treatise, another is the nature of a man — we are not free from passion.' If so, you, sir, ought to rescue the honorable <s>Rādhikā</s>, who is in such a state, from the ocean of grief. What do you say? — 'Whatever my friend commands — here are my joined palms — it would be good if I could be liberated [from this task].' Liberation is in every way hard for you to attain! But accept this benediction: [Verse 66:] Having returned from abroad, lift the yearning, bowed [woman] onto your lap; placing her face upon your shoulder, console the weeping one once more; then, having unfastened her braid, uneven [and rough] as a buffalo's horn, yourself cut the hanging curl that is greedily drinking the tear-water from your beloved's eyes. He has departed laughing. We go this way. (Walking about.) Ah, who indeed is this one approaching from this direction?

So be it — I have seen [him before]. This one was indeed seen before at the residence of my brother, or rather my friend, the honorable <s>Guptakula</s>, the jewel-offspring of the lord of the <s>Dāśeraka</s>s. So what is his purpose here? He approaches me with joined palms. What do you say? — [In Prakrit:] '<s>Guptakula</s> has sent [me to] look: "Go to the merchant-quarter in all directions [and see] if any courtesan desires [our patronage]; but on the main street, having looked everywhere, I see no courtesan at all worthy of him." Therefore [he says:] "Go play with them and report back." Ah, what an emissary of love for the young prince <s>Guptakula</s> — endowed with the excellence of regional costume, language, and courtesy! While actually being in the courtesans' quarter, he asks for the courtesans' quarter by the name 'merchant-quarter'! Such a gem cannot be enlightened and then destroyed — let him be as he is. I shall say this much to him: 'Good fellow, search for a courtesan in the salt-sellers' shops on the royal highway!' He has departed joyfully, bowing down. We go this way. (Walking about.) Where indeed can I now wash my eyes, shaken by the sight of the <s>Dāśeraka</s>? (Looking around.) So be it — I see it: for this is the dwelling of our former sweetheart, the beauty of <s>Śūrasena</s>. How [wonderful] — since its wing-doors are standing open, let me enter! (Having entered.) Where indeed can I now relieve the weariness of my feet from walking? So be it — I see it: this priyangu-vine arbor, like a beloved's lap, invites me with its stone seat. Let me sit down here. (Looking.) What has been written here? (Reading aloud:) [Verse 68:] 'Friend, at the first meeting there was no occasion for a quarrel; nor did I hear any dejection or bashfulness on his part. Having approached that young man, long desired by my heart — why has the design of body-paint returned unsmudged?' (Reflecting.) This is surely some woman's proclamation of misfortune — of one whose love has been rejected by someone. Whom shall I ask about this?

body.translated_text:
[p.102] (Lending an ear) Ah! This one, heralded by the sound of her foot-ornaments, is approaching — it is indeed the beauty of <s>Śūrasena</s>! For she —
(verse 69) Grasping with one hand, tender as a sprout, the lovely umbrella-staff, holding with the other her girdle-cord of trembling jewels, the hem of her garment slipping — she comes smiling, her body blazing ever brighter with the radiance of her ornaments, like the goddess of night, [adorned] with stars, with the moon, and with the cries of birds.
Oh, truly, her very radiance seems to make even me rise [in respect]! She approaches me with a pigeon [as a gift]. Enough of dismissing us with mere courtesies! What does the lady say? — 'Even after so long, when our lord has deigned to come, let this person at least honor herself by showing courtesy.' Enough, enough of excessive reproach! Let the lady favor [me by accepting] this proper seat upon my lap. She, saying 'I receive it with bowed head,' sits down, as if casting her broad hips onto half the stone slab. Oh, but one should not sit here! What does the lady say? — 'Why not?' Because we have seen here a verse-inscription — a record of disgrace — of some woman whose love was rejected by some [man]. What — she wipes [it] with her hands? O thief! This cannot be wiped away, for it is inscribed upon my heart! Does she now try to prevent [me from reading it]? What does the lady say? — 'Does our lord know about our friend <s>Kusumāvatikā</s>'s [feelings] toward her dear companion, the painting-master <s>Śivasvāmin</s>?'

[p.103] A great madness of love, [you mean]? We know that well. Moreover, has the honorable <s>Kusumāvatikā</s> favored the honorable [<s>Śivasvāmin</s>] with a visit? What does the lady say? — 'This is the nature of a woman's heart, distracted by love.' 'She has acted with womanly fickleness.' A curious topic of conversation indeed! Let us ask her then. My lady, it is trust that asks, not curiosity about another's secrets. So how was the festival of their long-desired union carried out? What does the lady say? — 'Listen then!' I am attentive. What does the lady say? — 'When she was favored by the honorable one under the pretext of wine-intoxication, then your friend's [night went thus]:'
(verse 70) The first watch passed with a tedious tale of wrestlers; the second was squandered on outside quarrels about meat and molasses; the third slipped away in talk about building up the body — as for what happened after that, enough said, if [one can say it] even to you!
Beautiful one, from whom did you learn this? What does the lady say? — 'Having learned the story from <s>Pratihāra Padmapāla</s>, who had come from that same friend's quarters, I sent this verse along by the hand of a cheerful messenger.' Then she herself came to me with that very attendant, laughing as if embarrassed and abashed.

[p.104] she told me. 'And I cannot do you the injustice of not telling you the secret — listen to this unprecedented tale!' And then she narrated to me everything as it happened. 'Therefore you too deserve to be regaled with this nectar for the ears.' She, clapping her hands and laughing heartily, narrates: 'Fair one, what do you say? — Listen now to what my dear friend told me. She said to me: "Dear friend, he was by me
(71a) embraced in many ways, kissed all over,
(71b) placed upon my lap, stimulated with my fingernails —
(71c) I was exhausted! Like a log, when he would not come to me,
(71d) I embraced a single limb of the bed and fell asleep."
Then I said to her: "Alas, you have suffered a hardship! Don't I understand this?" Then, sighing, she told me:
(72a) "When with every means and sweet words I approached him,
(72b) he, making no effort, could not obtain even the desire of the Love-god toward me.
(72c) Then, all my devices thwarted by him, I suddenly,
(72d) thinking it my own misfortune, wept with my breasts heaving."
Then he, lifting me as I wept onto his lap, repeatedly tried to console me with futile kisses and embraces, and earnestly exhausted himself. And I said to him: "What is wrong with you when touched by my hands?" Then

[p.105] trembling with the modesty-born diffidence, perspiration, and quivering, with a mouth as if drying up, he said in halting syllables:
(73a) "You should not blame yourself, O blameless, fortunate one;
(73b) for this eye of mine has fallen, gazing around at a treasure.
(73c) The <s>guggulu</s> (bdellium resin) that I once drank to reduce excess fat —
(73d) that very thing now destroys the nectar of union directed toward you."
Then I reflected:
(74a) If <s>guggulu</s> drunk to reduce fat
causes the loss of virility,
(74b) then even for incense purposes
it should not be used by a man in love!
Thus, our long-desired but fruitless union having reached its time, though both desiring it:
(75a) Announcing the night's departure,
(75b) the attendant at the king's kettledrum,
(75c) having struck the bell, recited
(75d) the benedictory morning praises — enough, dear friend!
Then, freed from that predicament by that same gallant as if by a kind friend, the lover, bashfully accompanied [by him] for a moment and then sent off, she came home.

[p.106] And you and [the other] with your pleasant-questioning pretense have mocked me! So this is everything told to you in full. 'I shall now dispel my false sleeplessness with a daytime nap!' — so saying, dismissed by me, she departed. And afterward my master too heard this story. Therefore, with this very raft of jest, I shall plunge into <s>Śivasvāmin</s>, son of the honorable <s>Śivadatta</s> — that ocean of reputation, deep with manly pretension. Watch, madam:
(76a) He who drinks <s>guggulu</s> when his fat has grown excessive —
(76b) his fat, O <s>Caṇḍī</s>, quickly diminishes;
(76c) but then he becomes, for women blooming with youth,
(76d) like a painted <s>Yakṣa</s> — delightful to look at, nothing more!
She, laughing, has risen — 'I shall go!' Very well, enough of salutations! We go this way. (Walking about.) What are these now — resembling groves of tall-stemmed white lotuses in their beauty — groups of courtesan-quarter maidens with upraised lotus-faces, eyes wide with wonder strung like garlands, hands placed upon their breasts, exchanging signals with one another, their ball-games and doll-and-daughter-play with tassel-fans abandoned — looking out along the courtesan-quarter street in the shadows of each mansion? What indeed is this?

body.translated_text: [p.107] (verse 77) This cask is rolling! Now a leather bag is being dragged! This headless trunk has risen and walks! Is it a pair of granaries? Could this be something wondrous? So be it — now it is recognized: that belly named <s>Upagupta</s> is creeping forth! Sirs, this is well said indeed in the assemblies of rogues: (verse 78) <s>Harikṛṣṇa</s>, his neck hidden by camel-humps, is truly a dark wild buffalo; <s>Haribhūti</s> the cow-buffalo; and <s>Upagupta</s> is a leather bag inflated by wind! And how indeed has that poor woman — the fan-bearer of [the establishment at] the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and <s>Yamunā</s>, the book-reader <s>Madayantī</s> — abandoned our dear friend, that elder learned in the three [<s>Vedas</s>], the book-reader, and become attached to <s>Upagupta</s>? And she embraces him with her delicate arms! Or rather, she has no need for his embrace — for that poor woman, having retired from the practice of love on account of the cessation of her menses, merely follows this 'word-lover' for the sake of household management. What do you say? — 'Then all the members of the assembly took <s>Upacandra</s>'s side. But I too championed <s>Mayūrasenā</s>'s cause.' Well done, friend! You acted suitably for the time and place. Then what? What do you say? — 'Then I did not insult their judgment. My assessors were not disrespected; by the authority of tradition (<s>āgama</s>), my position was established with the consent of the judges.'
[p.119] Well done, friend! The honorable lady was won over by a commodity unique to yourself. Then what? What do you say? — 'Then when the reward was given in the sight of all the courtesans, I felt as if favored by <s>Mayūrasenā</s>'s sidelong glance, preceded by a smile. But by <s>Kāverikā</s>'s manner — rising and leaving with a gesture betraying jealousy — I felt as if greatly reproached. And being a visible witness to both their anger and favor, as if fallen from both banks, carried along by the current of doubt, from that predicament I somehow came home. And sitting down, I swung the swing of deliberation, wondering what course to take with both of them. Then suddenly my beloved came and covered my eyes.' Then, laughing, I said:
(verse 98) O you who are skilled at covering eyes, what use is your secret laughter, O thief? The unique touch of your hands betrays you!
Thus addressed, she — with faltering syllables indicated by the fragrance of her sighs revealing intoxication — said to me: 'Tell me — who am I?' Then I said:

body.translated_text: [p.121] With her necklace slipped from one breast and resting against the pitcher-like side of the other, with an earring-<s>makara</s> that had slipped from her cheek now adorning the beauty-mark, in a pose more lovely with the turning of her shoulder — like <s>Rati</s> (the goddess of love) incarnate, with modesty as her sole companion — she scattered glances like water dappled with blue lotuses, with a single arched brow-vine, and said to me: 'As you please.' Then I, snatching the paint-and-color palette from a nearby window, presented myself to apply lac-dye to her lotus-feet. And then, friend — with my gaze fixed on the application of lac, I beheld the calf of her raised heel and ankle-belled leg, and because it was not yet consumed [by my gaze], and because the silk that followed the curves of the retraction at her thigh-joint was not pulled tight — I saw her inner thigh, like the pith of a young elephant's tusk, like the core of a plantain stem. And as I was gazing, she, pushing me away [and saying] 'You have immodest eyes!' — she raised her foot and struck me on the chest.

[p.122] Then, with skin rough from a coat of goosebumps, I said: 'Fair one, you should not dismiss me before the lac-application is finished!' Then she said to me: 'Very well then — close your eyes and finish it!' Then, with closed eyes, I applied the lac-dye to her feet. I was seized by the lower lip with a hair-pull. Then, looking at me thus, my goosebumps standing on end, [she said:] 'You are craving like an <s>aśoka</s> tree — homage to your trickery!' — and embracing me, she went to bed. What happened after that, only 'the beloved of the gods' will know! — If that is so, your honor too should attend upon the <s>viṭas</s> who have assembled for the penance of <s>Tauṇḍikoki Viṣṇunāga</s>. What do you say? — 'Perish the thought! Again — if only my head could be graced by the strike of her lotus-foot, that itself would be my penance!' If so, then like the serpent <s>Kāliya</s> — dwelling in the pool of the <s>Yamunā</s>, with forehead marked by the feet of the lord of the <s>Yadus</s> — you are now immune to punishment by all the <s>viṭas</s>, like [<s>Kāliya</s> was immune] to <s>Vainateya</s> (<s>Garuḍa</s>)! (verse 110) That one, mounted, with love-languid gestures, is embraced from behind by a woman who presses her breasts tightly against his back; turning around, he kisses his beloved as his horse, from habit, follows home by itself and does not stray from the path. And who is this one, present in this moonlight yet existing as though in darkness, standing in the bedroom-depths of the pleasure-quarter street, displaying his shamelessness? Ah, I know — this is the <s>Saurāṣṭrika Śaka</s> youth <s>Jayanandaka</s>, enamored of this barbarian [woman] <s>Ghaṭadāsī</s>. And what then has he [p.126] observed as the virtues of this pleasure-quarter barbarian in comparison with the entire courtesan-city? For this is that <s>Rākā</s>, who, embracing the king's brother-in-law, the <s>Ābhīraka</s> prince <s>Mayūrakumāra</s> — [who is] dancing like a peacock — displays her own good fortune on the terrace before the courtesans' street. And this poor fellow too has been purchased by her outright, as it were. [Verse 114:] And moreover, she — fair-skinned and stout — carries the dark, extremely thin <s>Mayūrakumāra</s> clinging to her breast, as if [carrying] the tip of her own shadow! (Walking about.) And who is this other one? (Reflecting.) This is she — the <s>Yavanī</s> (Greek/foreign woman) named <s>Karpūraturiṣṭhā</s>, the beloved of <s>Varāhadāsa</s>, son of the honorable <s>Śārdūlavarman</s> of auspicious name, our dear friend — who, holding with three fingers a bronze [cup] of honey facing the reflected moon, supporting an earring that has slipped to her cheek — its rays swinging — bears the moon, as it were, upon her shoulder. This one: [Verse 115:] The <s>Yavanī</s>, with eyes like a <s>cakora</s> bird's restless [glance], gazing at her face in the honey [mirror], parting with her nails the long vine-like curl of hair, wipes from her delicate cheeks — fair as <s>madhūka</s> blossoms — the flush of passion that has arisen, mistaking it for lac-dye. And moreover — a <s>Yavanī</s> courtesan, a monkey-woman dancer, a <s>Mālava</s> lover, a donkey singer — by their qualities I understand them to be equivalent. In every way, <s>Prajāpati</s> is indeed skilled in matching like with like! For indeed:

body.translated_text: [Verse 116:] The <s>ātmaguptā</s> vine [clings to] the <s>khadira</s> tree; the <s>paṭola</s> vine has embraced the <s>neem</s> — how fitting indeed is the union, if the <s>Yavanī</s> is attached to a <s>Mālava</s>! Well, although she too is my friend, I shall not address her. For who indeed would listen to those utterances of the courtesan-quarter <s>Yavanī</s>, which resemble the chatterings of a female monkey — full of hissing sounds, with unrecognizable expressions, with some obscure ulterior meanings, indicated merely by the fondling of the index finger? Enough of her! (Walking about.) And who is this other one? [Verse 117:] He who carries that beloved, her forelocks and upper garment swiftly lifted by the headwind, upon a she-elephant — like <s>Udayana</s> [carrying] <s>Vāsavadattā</s>! (Reflecting.) Ah, I know! This is that son of a rich man, called <s>Viṭapravāla</s> ('Sprout-Libertine') — a name bestowed by the buffoons — the lord of lovemaking-cloths and hip-garments, who, overpowered by passion, disregarding the commands of both father and mother, is enamored of that beauty of the courtesans' quarter, our own girl. He is indeed the ultimate buffoon! But we are embarrassed by the word 'father-in-law.' So enough of conversing with him.

body.translated_text: Here is a salute to him. We go this way. (Walking about.) Now let me too go to the <s>viṭa</s> assembly! Here I am, sirs — having traversed the well-traveled great highway of the courtesans' quarter, I have arrived at the mansion of <s>Bhaṭṭi Jīmūta</s>, the chief of libertines, whose front courtyard is crowded by thousands of vehicles of the libertine community assembled from all quarters, whose gateway is attended by servants offering water in raised silver vessels for foot-washing. Well indeed is it said: 'Great indeed are the undertakings of the great!' For now, flowers of five-and-a-half colors are being scattered; pearls are being strung and woven into garlands; incense is being circulated; lamps are being lit; 'Welcome!' is being said; vehicles are being released; coquetry is on display; songs are being sung; instruments are being played; hands are being offered; soft words are being spoken; warm embraces are given; [arms] are linked with affection; bows are made with modesty; the back of one who bows is touched; sidelong glances are exchanged; the head [of a guest] is smelled; [women] stand with graceful gestures; [guests] are seated playfully; sandalwood [paste] is distributed; color-cosmetics are applied; unguents are arranged; fragrant powder is scattered; jests are exchanged by the libertines; [offerings] are received by the coquettes — and in short: [Verse 118:] Stuck in flowers knee-deep, their feet are lifted with difficulty by the dwarves.

And here are these chief <s>viṭa</s>s — (verse 119a) Wealthy, with half-seats adorned by friends, (119b) making clever, non-wounding jests, (119c) surrounded on all sides equally by courtesans — (119d) like bulls in a cattle-pen, they shine with their attendants. And this is their assembly — (verse 120a) Like the sky with a hundred moons, [lit] by the moon-faces of women, (120b) its horizons made dappled by darting sidelong glances, (120c) as if [resounding] with the blows of young men's arms in combat, (120d) as if heaped with rocks — [by] their sandal-anointed chests. And moreover, in this [assembly] — (verse 121a) These shine as wish-granting trees for courtesan-folk — (121b) heroes of the moment and also root-plunderers — (121c) whose childhood quarrels (121d) the elders recount aloud, like [the quarrels] of <s>Suyodhana</s> and <s>Vṛkodara</s>. So then — having made an offering of joined palms to the lord <s>Citteśvara</s> upon my head, at my friend's command, I now undertake this task and, for the purpose of penance for the honorable <s>Tauṇḍikoki Viṣṇunāga</s>, I shall address the <s>viṭa</s>s with a formal proclamation. (Walking about.) Ho, ho!

body.translated_text: [p.131] All you quarrel-loving and quarrel-reporting rogue-sirs, assembled from every corner of the earth — hear ye, hear ye! (verse 122a) <s>Kāma</s> (Love) conquers even among ascetics, desirous of dominion, (122b) lord of all minds, master of the sense-steeds, (122c) whose command even the great beings bear (122d) with bowed heads whose crown-jewels' rays [shine bright]. (Walking about.) (verse 123a) And victorious is the intoxication of coquettes, (123b) scattering ear-ornaments through bursts of open laughter, (123c) with stumbling gait and unsteady, darting glances — (123d) and after that, the youthful charms are victorious! So, with my head purified by the dust from the feet of the chief courtesans, bowing before the rogue-sirs, I make this announcement. And what is this announcement? Hear — (verse 124a) Like a serpent, <s>Viṣṇunāga</s> (124b) writhes on the ground upon his chest; (124c) anxious for penance, (124d) you should deign to save him! What do the gentlemen ask? — 'What is his offense?' Hear — (verse 125a) With her hair tossed upward, tears flowing from the corners of her eyes, her eyebrow arched in anger, (125b) her lower lip bitten, her teeth flashing unsteadily, her face quivering, (125c) anklets jingling, pulling away with her hand her garment slipping with red-stained [lac], (125d) the beloved, in her passion, placed her foot — anklet and all — upon his head! What? What do the gentlemen say? — 'By whose [foot] was this unrecognized catastrophe to the man [inflicted]?'

body.translated_text: [p.132] This infamy called 'negligence' has spread far and wide! — Why, by none other than the honorable <s>Surāṣṭra</s> woman <s>Madanasenikā</s>! These <s>viṭa</s>s, as if startled [thinking] 'Fortunately no one is here [to witness this]' — who are they? (verse 126a) With hands thrown aside, suppressing their laughter, (126b) saying 'Shame!', composing stern faces, (126c) they contemplate, glancing at one another — (126d) as though seized by compassion, these rogues! Among those seated, the <s>viṭa</s> elder <s>Bhaṭṭi Jīmūta</s> has been appointed [judge]. He, overwhelmed with pity, has reached the utmost distress — this [one] here: (verse 127a) Releasing sighs of 'Alas, alas!', (127b) panting like an elephant, (127c) <s>Jīmūta</s> ('Cloud'), like a cloud, (127d) rains water from his two eyes. He summons me. Here I am — what does the lord command? — [<s>Bhaṭṭi</s>:] 'I have heard this before; you tell it again. So then, [the procedure] of approaching <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>s for penance [has been tried]. That is precisely why I am seated here. Let the venerable <s>viṭa</s>s be received with due formality.' As the lord commands! Ho, ho, hear ye, hear ye, gentlemen! (verse 128a) May he never win a wager at gambling! (128b) May he obey his mother and go with respect to his father!

body.translated_text: [p.133] (128cd) Let him drink boiled milk and eat a sweetmeat — but out of delusion, let him whose wife has been taken away speak what is improper here! Moreover: (verse 129) Let him serve his elders, let him depart from the assembly, let the disciplined youth become equal to an old man; upon seeing grey hair, let him go to peace — he who, seated here, would cite this as improper! (Turning and looking.) This <s>Dhārayaki</s> of endless tales, suddenly rising, calls me. What do you say? — 'This is indeed the sin of that woman whose love is unrecognized, not of this gentleman — you should hear: (verse 130) That foot which by its touch makes the <s>aśoka</s> tree blossom out of season, in which <s>Kāma</s> (the god of love) himself dwells with his bow and arrows drawn — that foot was placed on the head of a beast, as it were out of delusion by her; surely it is she, the fickle one, who should perform penance for a long time!' The gentleman speaks rightly; for indeed: (verse 131) This donkey has been serenaded with a lute; this monkey has been honored with verses; into buffalo-milk has been dropped the juice of mango! However, penances follow those in distress; and this man has come in distress — therefore, the honored sirs should deign to show him grace. Now where indeed is the patriarch of their clan?

These are the <s>viṭas</s>. But who is this one whose appearance is corrupted by his <s>viṭa</s>-nature? 'The foremost <s>viṭa</s>, rising in the <s>viṭa</s> assembly, presumes to prescribe a penance!' — they are angered. Hey, <s>Mallasvāmin</s>! Listen — this is what the honored gentlemen say. What do you say? — 'Wait, rather let the honored sirs be told: (verse 132) When my father died on the fifth day, when friends were distressed and the clan of relatives in confusion, taking up my one crying infant son, I drank liquor together with a slave-girl. How am I not a <s>viṭa</s>?' If so, they acknowledge you — you are a chief <s>viṭa</s>! Be seated. What do you say? — 'Let him be given a penance.' Very well, I shall announce it again. But now, who is this calling me? — The <s>Śaibyaka</s> poet <s>Āryarakṣita</s>, his syllables distorted by the disorder of his breath,

body.translated_text: [p.135] — no, no, this is not a [proper] penance! — protests. And this <s>Dhāntra</s> fellow is an arch-<s>viṭa</s>. Why? (verse 133) For he who, born in the <s>Śibi</s> clan, sells his poetry in the houses of <s>Śrotriya</s> Brahmins for a cup of wine — having grown old in the place of [his] patron! Moreover: (verse 134) If poets indeed nowadays sell their poetry for a cup of wine — in <s>Kāśī</s>, in <s>Kosala</s>, among the <s>Bhargas</s>, and in the city of <s>Niṣāda</s> — let me approach him. Friend, here I am! What do you say? — (verse 135) 'The mouthful of wine, held against the cheek like a lotus with a bee fastened to it, which, released by the coquette, makes the <s>bakula</s> tree blossom — that sport of the eyes, dear companion of the young mango — how shall that mouthful of wine reach the head of a beast?' Here is another — <s>Bhavakīrti</s>, with bound hands, calls me for his penance. And this young man is an arch-<s>viṭa</s>. Why? (verse 136) He who, having thrown to the ground a shaven, aged [nun] wearing worn ochre robes, who had entered fearlessly for alms, [leaving her] writhing in distress — this lustful fellow does as he pleases!

[p.136] Let me approach him then. What do you say? — 'This is the penance for her:'
(verse 137) Let her be bound with the cord of her girdle, having been dragged by the hair; and then, when she is asleep, let this man massage her feet!
Ha! This too is rejected! This rich man's son, called by the familiar name <s>Gāndharvasenaka</s> among the servants' children, raises his hand and summons me. He whose hand —
(verse 138) whose fingertips have been exercised in the three kinds of instruments with many techniques, who falls upon the strings like a shower of copper-lotus petals, who, holding the <s>vallakī</s> (lute) on the slope of his hip in the <s>kolamba</s> style — has savored the tossing of nails of the beauties from the inner chambers of the wealthy.
Let me approach him. (Approaching) What do you say? —
(verse 139) The triumphant banner of the buttocks upon the chariot of the hips, the <s>vīṇā</s> of the entangled union of love-making — where indeed is the jeweled girdle of noble women, and where are the feet of this wretched donkey!
(Turning around) Now this southern poet <s>Āryaka</s> prescribes a penance. What do you say? —
(verse 140) With the very gestures of flirtatious play, with profuse throwing of glances, upon his head with a lotus from behind the ear —

This too is rejected by this <s>Gāndhāraka</s>, this elephant-brained fool! What is this the gentleman says? —
(verse 141) Scratched by nails, adorned by a woman as a bond upon the ear, dappled with the imprint of sidelong glances hanging from the corner of the eye — if this is placed upon the head of this human beast, sirs, what penance could there be for him, [already] fragrant with pollen?
'Indeed, so it is!' — the chief <s>viṭa</s>s agreed. (Turning around) These two others summon me:
(verse 142) <s>Gupta</s> and <s>Maheśvaradatta</s>, two friends seated on one seat, their poetic talent aroused in the manner of <s>Vararuci</s>'s poetry.
Let me approach. (Approaching) Ho, hairy <s>Gupta</s>! What does the gentleman say? —
(verse 143a) 'Let his head be washed with the water from washing her feet!'
What — this too is vetoed? By <s>Maheśvaradatta</s>, honored by name among the elders versed in the three <s>Veda</s>s, our most excellent friend:
(verse 143b) 'He is not worthy even to drink the water from washing her feet!'

[p.138] Here is another friend of ours, an old <s>viṭa</s> from <s>Sauvīra</s>, who counsels with a speech preceded by an unconstrained smile. What does the gentleman say? —
(verse 144) '[Let her come] with her body-stalk made even lovelier by unadorned limbs, her hands of hair standing at her hips, released and wet from bathing — I shall bring her, and let this man hold before her a mirror dappled with the radiance of her eyes!'
This too is vetoed by the poet <s>Rudravarmā</s> of <s>Dāśeraka</s>. What do you say? —
(verse 145) 'This learned man, born in the great <s>Koki</s> lineage, minister in charge of counsels for the best of kings — he does not deserve to keep hair sprinkled with the dust from the feet of courtesans — let him be shaved!'
Now this <s>Viṣṇunāga</s>, saying 'I am indeed favored!', makes a petition: 'I desire this head — forever delighted and honored by the tread of the servant-girl's foot — to be cut off; but even before that, the hair!' How is this too overruled for him? By this greatest of <s>viṭa</s>s, <s>Bhaṭṭi Jīmūta</s>! What does the gentleman say? —
(verse 146) 'With the jingling sound of slipping bangles, of women with arched brow-creepers, inlaid with the rays of nails and the gleam of finger-rings — by the sprout-tender hands of beautiful women, let him keep his hair long untouched!'
Moreover, hear this penance for him:
(verse 147ab) Of that woman with eyes languidly rolling with intoxication, whose girdle is clasped by one hand placed on her hip —
